name: Rhythm
lede: Rhythm is a muted slate purple whose name has no documented origin; the color books mention rhythm only as a quality of color, never as a color.

sections.title: A name the books never use
sections.body:
*Rhythm* is a muted purple-grey, a slate with a little violet in it [9]. It comes from the Wikipedia list of color names, and its origin is undocumented in our data; the library marks it as an obscure or novelty name [9]. Our Japanese pairing for it, Benimidori, is only a nearest match, and has no connection to the English word [9].

None of the 29 color books uses it as a color name [8]. Every one of its 48 appearances in our search is the ordinary noun [8].

sections.title: Rhythm in writing about color
sections.body:
The noun does turn up in color writing, as a way of saying that colors move. Gage describes how Mondrian, in the 1920s, came to see rhythm as the unifying feature of life and art, drawing on jazz and the fox-trot [3]. Albers calls the changes of tempo or rhythm among his four-color studies a change of mood [4]. Pastoureau says Rothko plays with the rhythms of color to produce sonorous effects, so that several canvases hung together form a chromatic symphony [5].

Older writers made the music link too: in late antiquity Aristides argued that music reached body and soul through rhythms imitating bodily rhythms, which painting could not do [3]. The swatch's cool slate leaning to violet sits near [[slate]], [[purple-grey]] and [[lilac-grey]] in the library [9].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: As a painted color it is uncommon but not absent. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 48 works, about 0.2 per cent [10]. The best match is Krøyer's [[painting:smk-KMS8273|Skagen Beach in Moonlight]] of 1899, at 46 per cent of the canvas [10]. The 1900s are its peak decade, with 10 of 809 paintings, and [[painter:claude-monet|Monet]] and [[painter:edvard-munch|Munch]] each carry it in 3 of 50 works [10]. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a screen color, not a pigment test [10].
